spark.summary: LLM quantization compresses 16-bit model weights and KV caches into 8-bit or 4-bit representations (FP8, AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF) to slash VRAM usage by 2-4x and accelerate memory-bandwidth-bound token generation.
spark.keyTakeaway: Because autoregressive LLM decode is memory-bandwidth bound at low batch sizes, moving from FP16 to INT4/FP8 cuts HBM reads per token by 2-4x while keeping accuracy loss under ~1% when activation outliers are protected.

concept.whyItMatters: A 70B-parameter LLM in FP16 consumes ~140 GB just for weights—requiring two 80 GB H100s before serving a single token—and autoregressive decoding reads all 140 GB from HBM for every single generated token. Quantization fits that 70B model onto a single 48 GB or 80 GB GPU and multiplies decode throughput by shrinking memory traffic.
whenToUse: Serving 7B-70B+ models on fewer GPUs (e.g., fitting Llama-3.1-70B INT4 onto a single 80 GB A100/H100 instead of 2x GPUs).
Accelerating memory-bandwidth-bound decode latency (tok/s per user) in interactive chat and coding copilots.
Compressing long-context KV caches with FP8 (E4M3) to double or quadruple concurrent batch size at 32k-128k context.
whenNotToUse: Tiny models (<3B parameters) running at high batch sizes on H100s where inference is already compute-bound and INT4 dequantization overhead can hurt.
Sub-4-bit (INT2 / 1.58-bit) post-training quantization on complex reasoning or multi-step code generation without quantization-aware training (QAT).
Hardware lacking native INT8/FP8 Tensor Cores or fused dequantize-GEMM kernels (e.g., older GPUs running unoptimized INT4).
keyPoints: LLM inference has two distinct phases: compute-bound prefill (processing the prompt in parallel) and memory-bandwidth-bound decode (1 token at a time).
On an H100 (3.35 TB/s HBM3), reading 140 GB (FP16) caps batch-1 decode near ~24 tok/s, whereas 35 GB (INT4) raises the bandwidth ceiling near ~95 tok/s.
Activation outliers (~1% of channels with >6.0 magnitude) break naive Round-To-Nearest (RTN) INT4; AWQ, GPTQ, and SmoothQuant preserve those salient channels.
FP8 (E4M3) on Hopper/Ada Tensor Cores delivers near-lossless (<0.2% MMLU drop) W8A8 compute speedup for both prefill and decode.
KV-cache quantization (FP8/INT8) is often just as important as weight quantization at 32k+ context lengths where KV cache dominates VRAM.

examples.title: Single-GPU 70B Serving with AWQ + FP8 KV Cache
examples.scenario: A production team needs to serve Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct with 8k context on 80 GB A100 GPUs using vLLM.
examples.outcome: Using AWQ 4-bit weights (~38 GB VRAM) and FP8 KV cache leaves ~35 GB for paged KV blocks, fitting on 1 GPU instead of 2 and cutting per-token cost by ~50% with <0.8% benchmark drop.

examples.title: Naive RTN INT4 Collapse on Structured JSON Output
examples.scenario: A team applies naive Round-To-Nearest INT4 quantization without calibration to an 8B extraction model.
examples.outcome: Unscaled activation outliers distort attention projections, spiking JSON schema parse failures from 0.4% to 11%; switching to calibrated AWQ (128 calibration samples) restores 0.5% failure rate.

tradeOffs.pro: INT4 (AWQ/GPTQ/Q4_K_M) reduces weight memory by ~3.5-4x compared to FP16.
tradeOffs.con: Requires fused dequantize-GEMM kernels (Marlin/ExLlamaV2) and risks minor reasoning degradation on edge prompts.

tradeOffs.pro: W4A16 maximizes single-user decode speed by minimizing HBM reads.
tradeOffs.con: W8A8 (FP8) uses native Tensor Cores to accelerate compute-bound prefill and high-batch throughput, which W4A16 cannot.

tradeOffs.pro: AWQ/GPTQ calibration on 128-512 domain samples preserves accuracy much better than zero-shot RTN.
tradeOffs.con: Adds a 10-45 minute offline quantization step and requires domain-representative calibration text.

failureModes.name: Outlier Channel Clipping
failureModes.description: Naive min-max quantization scales an entire weight tensor to fit one extreme outlier, crushing normal weights into 1-2 bits.
failureModes.mitigation: Use group-wise quantization (group_size=128) paired with AWQ activation scaling or SmoothQuant.

failureModes.name: Dequantization Kernel Bottleneck at High Batch
failureModes.description: W4A16 models dequantize weights to FP16 in registers; at batch=64+, compute saturates and W4A16 becomes slower than FP8 W8A8.
failureModes.mitigation: Benchmark at target concurrency (e.g., batch=32 vs batch=1) and switch to FP8 W8A8 on H100/L40S for high-batch serving.

failureModes.name: Calibration Dataset Mismatch
failureModes.description: Calibrating GPTQ exclusively on English prose degrades accuracy on SQL, Python, or multilingual prompts.
failureModes.mitigation: Include a representative mix of code, JSON, and target-language samples in the 256-sample calibration set.

failureModes.name: KV-Cache OOM Under Long Context
failureModes.description: Compressing weights from 140 GB to 35 GB still OOMs if 100 concurrent 32k-token requests allocate 60+ GB of FP16 KV cache.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable PagedAttention with FP8 KV-cache quantization (--kv-cache-dtype fp8 in vLLM).

commonMistakes: Evaluating quantized models only on WikiText perplexity instead of task-specific evals like HumanEval, GSM8K, or strict JSON schema adherence.
Using W4A16 on H100s for high-concurrency batch workloads where FP8 W8A8 delivers higher total tokens/sec.
Forgetting to quantize the KV cache when serving 32k-128k context windows.
Deploying uncalibrated RTN INT4 instead of AWQ, GPTQ, or GGUF K-quants (Q4_K_M).
Ignoring kernel support—running GPTQ without Marlin or ExLlamaV2 kernels leaves 2-3x decode speed on the table.

sections.content:
## The idea

Autoregressive LLM generation is split into two physically opposite regimes. **Prefill** processes all prompt tokens in parallel as large matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMM), making it **compute-bound** (limited by Tensor Core TFLOPS). **Decode** generates one token per step per sequence, multiplying a thin activation vector against every weight matrix in the network—making it **memory-bandwidth bound**.

Quantization maps 16-bit floating-point numbers (`BF16`/`FP16`) onto smaller discrete grids (`FP8`, `INT8`, `INT4`) using affine scaling (`x_q = round(x / scale) + zero_point`). By shrinking weights 2x–4x, decode steps move 2x–4x fewer bytes across GPU HBM3 buses, directly multiplying tokens/sec while freeing VRAM for larger batches and longer KV caches.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose we deploy **Llama-3.1-70B** (`80 layers`, GQA `8` KV heads) on an **80 GB H100** (`3.35 TB/s` HBM3):

1. **FP16 baseline**: Weights alone require `70B * 2 bytes = 140 GB`, so it cannot fit on 1x H100. Across 2x H100s with tensor parallelism, batch-1 decode reads 140 GB/token.
2. **AWQ INT4 quantization (`group_size=128`)**: Using 256 calibration prompts, AWQ identifies the top ~1% salient weight channels (driven by large activation magnitudes) and scales them up before rounding to 4 bits. Packed weights drop to `~38 GB`.
3. **Fused Marlin kernel execution**: During decode in `vLLM`, the Marlin kernel loads packed INT4 weights from HBM (`38 GB` per pass), dequantizes them to FP16 inside GPU shared memory/registers on the fly, and multiplies against FP16 activations—cutting HBM traffic by ~3.7x.
4. **FP8 KV cache**: Enabling `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` halves KV-cache memory per token, leaving `~36 GB` for PagedAttention blocks.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Why naive rounding fails: activation outliers
sections.content:
## Why naive rounding fails: activation outliers

Transformer activations in models >6B parameters exhibit systematic **outlier features**: roughly 0.1%–1% of hidden dimensions consistently reach magnitudes 10x–100x larger than the median. Naive min-max quantization stretches the quantization grid to cover the outlier, squeezing 99% of normal values into a handful of buckets and destroying accuracy.

Modern schemes solve this in three ways:
- **LLM.int8()**: Keeps the ~0.1% outlier columns in FP16 and quantizes the remaining 99.9% to INT8.
- **SmoothQuant (W8A8)**: Migrates quantization difficulty from activations (`X`) into weights (`W`) via a diagonal scale `s`: `Y = (X diag(s)^-1)(diag(s) W)`.
- **AWQ (W4A16)**: Protects the top ~1% salient weight channels identified by activation magnitude without storing mixed-precision exceptions.

## Quantization schemes compared

| Format / Method | Bitwidth (W/A) | Memory vs FP16 | Hardware Target | Accuracy & Speed Profile |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **FP8 (E4M3)** | W8 / A8 | ~50% | H100, L40S, RTX 4090 | <0.2% drop; accelerates both prefill & decode |
| **AWQ (Marlin)** | W4 / A16 | ~28% | A100, H100, L4, 3090/4090 | <0.8% drop; fastest low-batch decode |
| **GPTQ (Marlin)** | W4 / A16 | ~28% | A100, H100, consumer GPUs | Hessian-aware rounding; strong at `group_size=128` |
| **GGUF (`Q4_K_M`)** | Mixed 4/6-bit | ~30% | Apple Silicon, CPU, llama.cpp | Mixed precision for attention/FFN sensitivity |
| **NF4 (QLoRA)** | W4 / BF16 | ~25% | Fine-tuning on 24-48 GB GPUs | Information-theoretically optimal for normal weights |

## Failure modes

Production deployments of quantized LLMs commonly fail in four ways:

- **High-batch W4A16 slowdown**: At batch sizes >32, W4A16's register dequantization adds ALU overhead that makes it *slower* than FP8 W8A8 on Hopper GPUs.
- **Silent tool-calling / JSON breakage**: Perplexity barely moves (+0.15), yet strict JSON bracket balancing or tool-argument extraction degrades noticeably on 3-bit or uncalibrated 4-bit models.
- **Missing fused kernels**: Loading a GPTQ checkpoint without `marlin` or `exllamav2` falls back to slow PyTorch dequantize-then-matmul, running slower than FP16.
- **Unquantized KV cache**: A 70B INT4 model serving 128k context still hits OOM if KV cache remains in FP16.

## How to benchmark before shipping

Never ship a quantized checkpoint on perplexity alone. Run a 3-layer gate:

1. **Task-specific evals**: Measure exact-match accuracy on your production prompts (tool calls, SQL, RAG citations) against the BF16 baseline.
2. **Throughput vs. concurrency curve**: Sweep concurrency (`1, 8, 32, 64, 128` requests) measuring Time-To-First-Token (`TTFT` p95) and Inter-Token Latency (`ITL` p95).
3. **VRAM headroom check**: Verify peak KV-cache utilization under max context length with PagedAttention enabled.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Choose **FP8 (W8A8)** on H100/L40S when serving medium-to-high batch concurrency; choose **AWQ + Marlin (W4A16)** for single-GPU 70B or low-latency decode.
- [ ] Enable **FP8 KV-cache** (`--kv-cache-dtype fp8`) for workloads with >8k average context length.
- [ ] Calibrate AWQ/GPTQ on 128–512 domain-matched samples (including code/JSON if used in production).
- [ ] Confirm fused kernels (`Marlin`, `FlashInfer`, `CUTLASS FP8`) are active in engine startup logs.
- [ ] Run end-to-end JSON schema, tool-calling, and RAG faithfulness regressions against the FP16/BF16 baseline.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: LLM quantization compresses 16-bit model weights and KV caches into 8-bit or 4-bit representations (FP8, AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF) to slash VRAM usage by 2-4x and accelerate memory-bandwidth-bound token generation.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Fused Dequant-GEMM applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Paged FP8 KV Cache.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Paged FP8 KV Cache experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use group-wise quantization (group_size=128) paired with AWQ activation scaling or SmoothQuant.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Because autoregressive LLM decode is memory-bandwidth bound at low batch sizes, moving from FP16 to INT4/FP8 cuts HBM reads per token by 2-4x while keeping accuracy loss under ~1% when activation outliers are protected.
Avoid trap: Evaluating quantized models only on WikiText perplexity instead of task-specific evals like HumanEval, GSM8K, or strict JSON schema adherence.
Avoid trap: Using W4A16 on H100s for high-concurrency batch workloads where FP8 W8A8 delivers higher total tokens/sec.
When to reach for it: Serving 7B-70B+ models on fewer GPUs (e.g., fitting Llama-3.1-70B INT4 onto a single 80 GB A100/H100 instead of 2x GPUs).
When to reach for it: Accelerating memory-bandwidth-bound decode latency (tok/s per user) in interactive chat and coding copilots.

putItTogether.title: Putting Quantization And Llm Inference Together
putItTogether.summary: Because autoregressive LLM decode is memory-bandwidth bound at low batch sizes, moving from FP16 to INT4/FP8 cuts HBM reads per token by 2-4x while keeping accuracy loss under ~1% when activation outliers are protected.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Quantization And Llm Inference before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.

putItTogether.outcome: Using AWQ 4-bit weights (~38 GB VRAM) and FP8 KV cache leaves ~35 GB for paged KV blocks, fitting on 1 GPU instead of 2 and cutting per-token cost by ~50% with <0.8% benchmark drop.
